title: Jhumka vs chandbali vs studs: picking earrings for ethnic wear
description: Jhumka, chandbali or studs? A practical guide to which earring suits which outfit, neckline, hairstyle and occasion, plus comfort tips for long events.
intro: Wear jhumkas when you want a playful, traditional look that moves, chandbalis when you want drama around the face, and studs when the outfit or the neckpiece should do the talking. The right pick depends less on the earring itself and more on your neckline, hairstyle and how long you will be wearing it. Here is how to decide.

sections.heading: What each style actually is
paragraphs: A jhumka is a bell or dome-shaped earring that hangs from a stud or a hook, often with small beads or pearls along the rim. The bell swings as you move, which is a big part of its charm.

A chandbali takes its name from the crescent moon (chand) shape. It is flat and wide, usually open at the top and curved at the bottom, and frames the side of the face. Chandbalis are often worked in Kundan, Polki-look stones or Meenakari enamel, with drops hanging from the lower edge.
Studs sit on the earlobe without hanging. In ethnic jewellery they range from tiny single stones to large floral Kundan studs that cover the whole lobe.

sections.heading: Match the earring to the neckline
paragraphs: Neckline is the most useful starting point, because it decides how much empty space there is between your ears and shoulders.
list: Boat neck and high neck: the neck is covered, so a long earring has room to shine. Chandbalis and long jhumkas both work; skip a necklace.
Deep V or sweetheart neck: you will probably wear a necklace here, so balance it. Medium jhumkas or studs keep the look from getting crowded.
Round neck kurta: almost anything works. Jhumkas are the classic pairing.
Collared or bandhgala neck: studs or small jhumkas. A big chandbali fights with the collar.
Off-shoulder or strapless blouse: chandbalis or statement jhumkas fill the space beautifully.

sections.heading: Which one for which occasion
paragraphs: For a puja at home, a family lunch or a temple visit, jhumkas are the easy favourite. They look traditional without feeling overdone, and small oxidised or Meenakari ones suit cotton sarees and kurtas.

For a sangeet, reception or festive party, chandbalis earn their place. They catch light, show up well in photographs and look complete even without a heavy necklace. If you are wearing a big necklace set, pick the matching earrings that come with it rather than adding a second statement.

For the wedding day itself, or any look built around a heavy choker or rani haar, studs or small drops let the neckpiece lead. Brides often wear larger earrings with a supporting chain (sahara) to take the weight off the lobe.
For office or college ethnic days, studs are the practical choice. They do not catch on dupattas or hair and nobody gets distracted by jingling during a meeting.

sections.heading: Hair and face decide the size
paragraphs: With a bun or a braid, all three styles are fully visible, so you can go bold. With open hair, small studs vanish; a chandbali or a jhumka with some length shows through better.

Face shape matters too. Chandbalis are wide, so they flatter long and heart-shaped faces. Long jhumkas that drop below the jaw suit round faces. Studs work on everyone, but large floral studs look best on longer faces.

sections.heading: Comfort over a long day
paragraphs: Weight is the hidden problem with ethnic earrings. A heavy chandbali can feel fine at 7 pm and painful by midnight. Before a long event, wear the pair at home for an hour. If the lobe starts to droop or ache, take a light pair as a backup in your bag.

Check the back closure. Push-back studs should fit snugly; a loose one is how earrings get lost on a dance floor. For heavier jhumkas, a silicone back or a small clear lobe-support patch helps them hang straight.
If you have sensitive skin, keep wearing time short for any plated earring and wipe the post before and after use.

sections.heading: Owning one of each
paragraphs: If you are building a collection, start with one pair of each in a neutral finish such as gold-tone Kundan, which goes with most colours. Studs cover everyday and office, jhumkas cover pujas and family functions, and chandbalis cover parties and weddings. Our [Kundan and Meenakari earrings](/women/earrings) are a budget-friendly way to try a style before committing to a bigger set, and the [Kundan necklace sets](/women/necklaces) come with matched earrings if you want the pairing done for you. Store each pair separately in a small pouch so jhumka beads and chandbali drops do not tangle.

faq.q: Are jhumkas or chandbalis better for a saree?
faq.a: Both work. Jhumkas suit cotton and silk sarees for day events; chandbalis suit heavier silk or georgette sarees for evening functions.

faq.q: Can I wear chandbalis with a necklace?
faq.a: Yes, but keep one of them lighter. A big chandbali pairs best with a delicate chain, or with the matching set it came with.

faq.q: Which earrings are best for a long wedding day?
faq.a: Lightweight jhumkas or medium studs. If you want chandbalis, use a lobe support or a chain so the weight is shared.

faq.q: Do studs look too plain with ethnic wear?
faq.a: Not if you choose a large Kundan or Meenakari stud. They look polished and let the outfit or necklace stand out.
